summary: Describes MIKEY, a key management scheme for real-time multimedia, covering both two-party and group communication. Its main use is providing keys to the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP), so encrypted calls and streams can start with shared secrets set up efficiently.

eli5.summary: Before two people can talk in a secret code, they must agree on the code. This document is a quick way for call and video apps to agree on it.

subtitle: A lightweight key management protocol that sets up encryption keys for calls and streams in one round trip.

tldr.problem: Security protocols for real-time multimedia, such as SRTP, need keys and parameters agreed before media flows. Existing schemes such as IKE were not seen as low-latency enough for real-time data over mixed wired and wireless networks and for small interactive groups.
tldr.mechanism: MIKEY has the Initiator send one message that carries a random value, a timestamp and a TEK Generation Key (TGK), protected by a pre-shared key, a public key, or a Diffie-Hellman exchange. Both sides then derive the traffic-encrypting keys from the TGK.
tldr.outcome: MIKEY is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4738 and RFC 6309. Its main described use is providing keys and policies to SRTP.

facts.label: Minimum RAND
facts.value: At least 128 bits for key derivation; RAND length SHOULD be at least 16 bytes

today: RFC 3830 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 4738 and RFC 6309. It remains the base specification for MIKEY as described in the text.

sections.title: The Problem MIKEY Solves
sections.content:
The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) protects real-time media, but a security protocol still needs a way to exchange keys and related parameters. MIKEY (Multimedia Internet KEYing) is that key management scheme. It targets multimedia setups such as SIP calls and RTSP sessions, in heterogeneous networks that mix wired and wireless links.

The RFC notes that IKE is a widely accepted unicast scheme for IPsec and that other IETF work addresses group communication, but argues there is still a need for lower latency. The SDP k= field can carry a key but cannot be extended into general key management.

MIKEY is mainly meant for peer-to-peer calls, simple one-to-many streaming and small interactive groups. Its design goals are end-to-end security (only the participants get the keys), simplicity, and efficiency (low bandwidth, low computation, small code size and a minimal number of round trips). It should also be possible to tunnel MIKEY inside session setup protocols such as SDP and RTSP, and it does not depend on security features of the underlying transport.
sections.eli5: Two friends need a secret handshake before a private phone call. MIKEY is a fast way to teach them the same handshake.

sections.title: Crypto Sessions, TGKs and TEKs
sections.content:
MIKEY's goal is to produce a Data Security Association (Data SA) for the security protocol: a traffic-encrypting key (TEK) plus a set of parameters and policies. The TEK is derived from a TEK Generation Key (TGK), a bit-string the parties agree on. From one TGK, many TEKs can be generated without more communication.

A Crypto Session (CS) is one or more data streams protected by a single instance of a security protocol. With SRTP, a CS typically contains an RTP stream and its RTCP stream. Several Crypto Sessions form a Crypto Session Bundle (CSB), which can share a TGK and security parameters but obtains distinct TEKs. Each CS has an identifier within its CSB, and each CSB has its own ID.

The procedure has three steps. First, security parameters and TGKs are agreed for the CSB by one of three methods. Second, the TGK is used to derive a TEK for each Crypto Session. Third, the TEK and the security protocol parameters make up the Data SA that is handed to the security protocol. The Initiator of MIKEY is not necessarily the one who initiates the communication.
sections.eli5: One master secret is agreed once. From it, each call stream gets its own lock key, so the master secret never has to be sent again.

sections.title: Three Ways to Transport or Exchange a Key
sections.content:
Each method sends a timestamp, to avoid replay, and a random value called RAND, which is always in the Initiator's first message. TGKs and RAND then feed key derivation.

Pre-shared key. The Initiator sends HDR, a timestamp, RAND, optional IDs, security policies and a KEMAC payload. KEMAC holds the TGK(s) encrypted with a key derived from the shared secret, followed by a MAC over the whole message. A verification message back from the Responder is optional and gives mutual authentication; the Initiator says in the header whether it wants one. This method is the most efficient because it uses only symmetric cryptography, but it scales poorly to large groups. Implementing it is MANDATORY.

Public-key encryption. The Initiator picks a random envelope key and sends it encrypted under the Responder's public key (the PKE payload). The TGKs, with the Initiator's identity, are encrypted under keys derived from the envelope key, and the whole message is signed (SIGN). It scales better but costs more, and usually needs a PKI. The envelope key can be cached and used later as a pre-shared key, for example to add a crypto session. Implementing it is MANDATORY.

Diffie-Hellman. Each side sends a signed DH value, and the TGK is g^(xi*xr). This costs more in computation and bandwidth and needs certificates, but it offers perfect forward secrecy. It creates one unpredictable key per pair, so it cannot make a group key. The Initiator chooses the group parameters, and implementing the method is OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to share the secret: already own the same key, lock it in a box only your friend can open, or both mix colors so a secret appears that was never sent.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Mandatory Algorithms
sections.content:
All key derivation uses one pseudo-random function (PRF) built from HMAC with SHA-1, a simplified version of the one in TLS. It takes an input key, a label and the wanted output length. To derive keys from a TGK, the label is a constant, then the crypto session ID, the CSB ID and RAND. The constant picks the key type: TEK, authentication key, encryption key or salting key. A similar derivation produces the encryption, authentication and salt keys used inside MIKEY itself from the pre-shared or envelope key. RAND must be at least 128 bits for these derivations.

The RFC lists defaults that every implementation must support. SHA-1 is the mandatory hash. Key data is encrypted with AES in counter mode using a 128-bit key, and the MAC is HMAC-SHA-1 with a 160-bit tag. For the public-key method, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 is mandatory for encryption and signatures, and RSA OAEP and RSA PSS are recommended. When Diffie-Hellman is supported, the OAKLEY 5 group is mandatory, while OAKLEY 1 and OAKLEY 2 are optional. AES key wrap is an optional encryption choice.

NULL encryption and NULL authentication exist for special SIP cases where SDP is already protected end to end. They MUST NOT be used unless the underlying protocols guarantee security, and the RFC says to use them with caution. Timestamps use the 64-bit NTP format, and new transforms are added by registering numbers with IANA.
sections.eli5: A recipe turns one master secret into many separate keys. Everyone has to use the same recipe and the same basic tools so their results match.

sections.title: Messages and Payloads
sections.content:
A MIKEY message is a Common Header payload (HDR) followed by a chain of payloads, each naming the next in a next payload field. A MAC or signature payload comes last. Payloads are byte aligned, not 32-bit aligned, and use network byte order.

The header carries the version (0x01 for this document), a data type for the message kind, the V flag that asks for a verification message, the PRF function, the 32-bit CSB ID, the number of crypto sessions and a map that ties crypto sessions to security protocol sessions. The only map type defined is the SRTP ID, with a policy number, SSRC and rollover counter per stream.

Other payloads include the key data transport payload (KEMAC), envelope data (PKE), DH data, signature, timestamp, identity and certificate, certificate hash, verification message, security policy, RAND and error payloads, plus key data sub-payloads and a general extension payload. The SRTP security policy lets a sender negotiate items such as encryption algorithm, authentication algorithm, key lengths, key derivation rate, authentication tag length and the order of FEC and SRTP. Key validity is given either by an SPI or MKI or by an interval. IANA is asked to manage the name spaces for these fields and to register the application/mikey media type.
sections.eli5: A MIKEY message is a stack of labeled envelopes in a fixed order. The first envelope says what is inside the others.

sections.title: Rekeying, Replay Protection and Errors
sections.content:
MIKEY can update a bundle by running again, for example before a TEK expires or to add a crypto session. An update reuses the same CSB ID but must carry a new timestamp, and it MUST NOT include a new RAND. Certificates and other static payloads may be left out, and an update need not carry new key material. The RFC notes that this is updating by ordinary unicast messages, not re-keying in the group key management architecture sense.

MIKEY uses timestamps instead of challenge-response, so clocks must be loosely synchronized. A Responder keeps a replay cache of messages it has successfully authenticated within an allowed clock skew, and discards replayed or outdated messages. The RFC describes the tradeoff: a larger cache allows looser clocks. As an example, 6 kB of cache at 30 bytes per message holds about 204 messages. Only authenticated messages are stored. Using timestamps keeps the exchange to at most one round trip.

On receiving a message, the recommended order is to check the timestamp and replay cache, find the identity and algorithms, verify the MAC or signature, and then process. Errors SHOULD be reported with an error message, which can also list the supported security policies so the Initiator can pick a common set. For authentication failures the error message is optional and need not be authenticated, since a signed error reply could be used for denial of service and an unauthenticated one could be used to trick the Initiator into tearing down the bundle.
sections.eli5: Messages carry a time stamp, like a ticket with today's date. The receiver keeps a list of tickets it has seen, so a copied old ticket does not work.

sections.title: Transport, Groups and SRTP
sections.content:
MIKEY may be integrated into session setup protocols; its use inside SIP/SDP and RTSP is defined in a separate document that the RFC cites, and other transports may be used if how is defined. MIKEY itself does not send network addresses or ports, since they may not be known in advance and NATs can interfere. For SRTP, the SSRC is used to find the Data SA, and the RFC recommends also matching on destination address and port.

For groups, MIKEY works in two settings. In a simple one-to-many case, a streaming server acts as Initiator and sends the same TGK to all clients using the pre-shared or public-key method, using the same CSB ID and crypto session IDs for all. Members need a common security policy, which limits negotiation, and requesting a verification reply from every receiver can load the Initiator as the group grows. In a small interactive group with no central controller, each client sets up the security for its own outgoing streams, with unicast SRTP between clients. The Diffie-Hellman method cannot be used for group keys.

Appendix A maps MIKEY terms to SRTP: a Crypto Session is an SRTP stream, the Data SA is the input to SRTP's crypto context, and the TEK is the SRTP master key. If an MKI is present in an SRTP packet it points to the correct key; if the key sent was a TGK, MIKEY derives the TEK before SRTP uses it.
sections.eli5: For a few friends on one call, each person tells the others the secret for their own voice. A shared stream can hand everyone the same secret at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's guiding rule is that no chain is stronger than its weakest link: the key exchange must give at least the protection that the media encryption needs. Key sizes should be weighed against the TGK size, and random numbers for TGKs must be good, because in the pre-shared and public-key methods a single party (the Initiator) generates the TGK. Neither of those provides perfect forward secrecy. Only the Diffie-Hellman method does, and it needs authentication such as signatures to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. If a TGK leaks, every TEK from it is compromised, but one TEK leaking does not expose the others.

Random RAND values counter off-line pre-computation attacks. Because updates reuse the old RAND, the RFC works out that many updates lose some effective entropy, and argues that this is not a practical problem for a properly chosen key size. Each security protocol must also bound how much data a key protects; for SRTP, the TEK and TGK must be changed at least every 2^48 SRTP packets.

For denial of service, a Responder builds no key management state before it authenticates the Initiator, but spoofed requests are still possible and the transport can validate addresses. The Initiator's message should include the Responder's identity (IDr), which is highly recommended. A CPU attack that makes the target verify many MACs or signatures is regarded as more serious than filling the replay cache. Identity protection was not a main goal. Finally, an insecure session setup protocol can indirectly affect secured media, and for groups the RFC recommends data origin authentication, such as digital signatures, in the security protocol.
sections.eli5: A chain breaks at its weakest link, so the lock for the key must be as strong as the lock for the call. Only the mix-colors method keeps old calls safe if a key leaks later.
